title: Analyzing and comparing complex environmental time series using a cumulative sums approach
author: Regier, Briceño, et al.
materials: creating random gaps in the dataset;

steps.title: Download raw data
steps.instruction: Access the Florida Coastal Everglades LTER online database (http://fcelter.fiu.edu/data/core) and download the daily total phosphorus (TP) concentration dataset LT_ND_Grahl_001 (and optionally salinity and water level datasets LT_ND_Grahl_001 and PHY_Grahl_002).

steps.title: Bin to monthly means
steps.instruction: Convert the daily TP values to monthly arithmetic means, producing a time series of one value per month.

steps.title: Standardize data
steps.instruction: Calculate the mean (m) and standard deviation (σ) of the monthly TP series, then compute standardized values zi for each month using zi = (xi – m) / σ.

steps.title: Compute Cusum series
steps.instruction: Generate the cumulative sum series (Cusum) by applying zis = zi + zis‑1 for each month (initialize z0 = 0).

steps.title: Plot results
steps.instruction: Create three plots: (A) original monthly TP series with the mean line, (B) standardized series (zi), and (C) Cusum series (zis). Use different colors to indicate values above or below the mean.

steps.title: Normalize for NSE
steps.instruction: Rescale the original TP series to the 0–1 range (min‑max normalization) before any NSE calculations.

steps.title: Calculate NSE
steps.instruction: In R, load the hydroGOF package and compute the Nash‑Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) between the original Cusum series and each manipulated Cusum series using the formula NSE = 1 – Σ(observed‑predicted)² / Σ(observed‑mean)².

steps.title: Test data‑gap robustness
steps.instruction: Randomly remove (a) 50 % and (b) 75 % of the monthly TP points, recompute the Cusum for each reduced dataset, and calculate NSE values (50 % removal NSE = 0.968; 75 % removal NSE = 0.792).

steps.title: Test distribution robustness
steps.instruction: Transform the original TP series using (a) square‑root, (b) square, and (c) log10. For each transformed series, recompute the Cusum and calculate NSE (all > 0.945; specific values: square‑root NSE = 0.945, square NSE = 0.946, log10 NSE = 0.945).

steps.title: Test noise robustness
steps.instruction: Generate white‑noise values with a range equal to twice the TP mean (mean = 0.68 mg L⁻¹): • 100 % noise range –0.68 to +0.68 mg L⁻¹, • 200 % noise range –1.36 to +1.36 mg L⁻¹, • 1000 % noise range –6.80 to +6.80 mg L⁻¹. Add each noise set to the original TP series, recompute Cusums, and calculate NSE (100 % NSE = 0.985; 200 % NSE = 0.954; 1000 % NSE = 0.735).

steps.title: Prepare driver‑response data
steps.instruction: For a chosen driver variable (e.g., water level), sort its observations in ascending order; reorder the paired response variable (TP or salinity) to match this driver order.

steps.title: Cusum‑transform response
steps.instruction: Apply the Cusum calculation (Eq. 2) to the reordered response variable, producing a Cusum‑transformed response series.

steps.title: Plot driver‑response relationships
steps.instruction: Create two plots for each response: (a) original response vs. untransformed driver (gray), and (b) Cusum‑transformed response vs. untransformed driver (red).

steps.title: Identify threshold points
steps.instruction: Locate the water‑level value where the Cusum slope changes sign (negative to positive for TP, positive to negative for salinity); report the approximate threshold (≈ 40 cm water depth).

description: It is important to note limitations to the format of data compatible with the Cusum techniques described above, particularly irregular time intervals between sampling events. Since neither Eq. (1) or Eq. (2) incorporates the time interval between data points, regular sampling intervals are assumed. However, irregular sampling frequencies due to any number of potential limitations (e.g. seasonal lack of access to site, ice-over of aquatic sites, etc.) are common in environmental studies. This issue is illustrated in Fig. 2, where holes were randomly punched in the time series. The authors do observe some deformation of the Cusum shape, although NSE statistics in Table 1 indicate minimal change when half the data are randomly removed, and, even with 75% of the data randomly removed, the resulting Cusum is still well predicted (based on the previously discussed NSE threshold of 0.65 in the literature). It has also been documented that Cusum-transformed time series are not appropriate for linear regression, where the Cusum transformation increases auto-correlation in a time series, violating linear regression assumptions that data are independently sampled and identically distributed [27]. As such, applying linear regression modeling to two Cusum-transformed time series can result in spuriously high correlations. In the two examples of Cusum plot types presented in this manuscript, the variable on the y-axis is Cusum-transformed, while the variable on the x-axis is not, and we are not applying linear regression analysis. However, the authors caution that users of the Cusums methodology should be aware of potential limitations discussed in this section before using the technique.
